rows: What is Berlin-Kay's universal color naming sequence?
Black/white → red → yellow or green → the other → blue → brown → pink/orange/purple/gray
What did Homer's wine-dark sea reveal?

Ancient Greek had no basic blue term. Gladstone noticed Homer never uses blue for the sky. Geiger identified this across multiple ancient language families — blue term follows available blue materials.
Does lacking a blue word mean you can't see blue?
No — Himba people can discriminate blue from green. But they're slower at it and group them together in categorization tasks. Language affects ease of discrimination, not raw sensitivity.
Why did "orange" not exist as an English color name before ~1500?
The fruit arrived from Asia; the color borrowed the fruit's name. Before then: "yellow-red." The color name follows the naming of a familiar object of that color.
What is the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (color version)?

Weak form confirmed: language shapes categorical perception speed. Russian speakers discriminate siniy/goluboy blues faster than English speakers at the siniy/goluboy boundary. Strong form (can't perceive what you can't name) rejected.
The best example of a color category — more consistent across cultures than category boundaries. Everyone agrees on "the best red" before they agree on where red ends.
